claims.text: Rapid deposition introduces inherent microstructural disorder and fine-scale multiphase or inhomogeneously ordered regions into non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys.
This deposition-induced disorder and fine-scale multiphase structure govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
The as-deposited material has a fine grain structure.
Low-temperature post-deposition annealing promotes partial chemical ordering.
Low-temperature post-deposition annealing coarsens the microstructure while retaining a high surface-to-volume ratio.
Annealing below the transformation onset for a short duration can avoid complete ordering and excessive grain coarsening.
Nanoscale twin boundaries or ordered domains act as nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Controlled annealing changes the density and distribution of nanoscale twin boundaries or ordered domains.
Changing the balance between disordered and ordered regions smooths the distribution of energy barriers associated with the magnetostructural transition.
Smoothing the energy-barrier distribution broadens the magnetostructural transition.
Broadening the transition reduces hysteresis by making the first-order event less sharp.
Mild annealing preserves a significant magnetocaloric entropy change.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will exhibit a less abrupt and more gradual magnetocaloric transition.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will exhibit significantly reduced hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealing may slightly shift the transition temperature.
The stated baseline materials display a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
The stated baseline materials have limited heat-exchange performance.
Annealing beyond the mild-intervention regime can cause excessive grain growth or full ordering and thereby alter the predicted effect.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as rapidly deposited material, but the baseline calls both arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons 'as-deposited.' Arc-melted ingots are not ordinarily a deposited form, and they do not share the high surface-to-volume geometry attributed to rapidly deposited ribbons or films.

A transition-temperature shift is presented only as a possible observation, yet absence of such a shift is included as a falsifying result. An optional prediction cannot by itself supply a valid falsification criterion.

The mechanism predicts preservation of a significant entropy change, not necessarily a significant change in entropy relative to baseline, whereas the falsification rule treats no significant change in magnetocaloric entropy as falsifying.
